slides.headline: The tallest flying bird is as tall as you.
slides.sub: Meet the sarus crane of north India's wetlands and rice fields

slides.label: standing height of a sarus crane
slides.body: That is about 5.9 feet, the tallest of the flying birds. Its wings can span 2.5 m and it weighs 5–12 kg.

slides.headline: At home in farm country
slides.body: They have adapted to farmland, especially low wetlands and flooded rice paddies. In India most live along the Gangetic plain and in eastern Rajasthan.

slides.headline: Pairs dance and trumpet
slides.body: Pairs dance with loud trumpeting calls. It has been suggested they mate for life, though little research has tested the claim.

slides.headline: A nest like an island
slides.body: Pairs build enormous nests of reeds and grasses in wetlands, often looking like islands. A clutch is usually two or three eggs.

slides.headline: Vulnerable, and declining
slides.body: IUCN lists the sarus crane as Vulnerable (2016), with an estimated 13,000–15,000 mature birds and a decreasing trend.

slides.headline: Send this to a birdwatcher.
slides.body: Near a flooded paddy, look for the red head. Follow @earthspirit_nature.

caption:
The sarus crane (Antigone antigone) is considered the tallest flying bird, standing about 1.8 m.

Its bare red head and upper neck sit on a pale grey body, so a pair is easy to pick out across a field. Breeding pairs prefer to forage in natural wetlands, but they also feed in wet rice and wheat crops and take small aquatic animals.

Swipe to size it up. Sources on the last slide.

Source: IUCN Red List (2016); Animal Diversity Web.
